hints: Picture what magnesium atoms do with their two outer electrons when packed together as a metal, and what charged particles are left behind in fixed positions.
Think about where those released electrons go and what word describes electrons that are free to move through the whole structure rather than fixed to one atom.
walkthrough:
Build the picture of a metal from atoms**
Imagine magnesium atoms packed closely together. Each Mg atom loses its two outer electrons to become $\text{Mg}^{2+}$. So you are left with positive ions sitting in regular rows, like oranges stacked in a box.

Place the electrons correctly**
Those lost electrons do not stay with one ion. They spread out and move freely in the spaces all around the ions. Draw small $e^{-}$ symbols all around the large $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ circles, or shade the background and label it electrons. Then add the vital label delocalised electrons to show they belong to the whole lattice.

Final answer: Regular lattice / rows of $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ions (minimum 4 ions in two rows) surrounded by a sea of electrons.
Labels: ions / cations / $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and delocalised electrons / sea of electrons.

hints: Recall the two standard general equations: metal with acid gives salt plus what gas, and carbonate with acid gives salt plus which two products.
Apply those patterns to $\text{Mg} + \text{HCl}$ and $\text{MgCO}_{3} + \text{HCl}$, remembering the salt in both cases is already given as $\text{MgCl}_{2}$.
walkthrough:
Sort reaction 1 as metal plus acid**
$\text{Mg} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}$. A reactive metal displaces hydrogen from the acid, so apart from $\text{MgCl}_{2}$ you get bubbles of hydrogen, $\text{H}_{2}$.

Sort reaction 2 as carbonate plus acid**
$\text{MgCO}_{3} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_{2} + \text{CO}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. All metal carbonates react this way with acids, so apart from $\text{MgCl}_{2}$ you get carbon dioxide, $\text{CO}_{2}$, and water, $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.

Final answer: reaction 1: hydrogen / $\text{H}_{2}$
reaction 2: carbon dioxide / $\text{CO}_{2}$ AND water / $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

hints: Compare the solubilities of $\text{Mg(OH)}_{2}$, $\text{Ca(OH)}_{2}$ and $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2}$ and recall how solubility of Group 2 hydroxides changes down the group.
walkthrough:
Link precipitate to insolubility**
A precipitate only appears if the product is insoluble. $\text{Mg(OH)}_{2}$ is almost insoluble, so adding $\text{OH}^{-}$ ions from $\text{Ca(OH)}_{2}(\text{aq})$ forces white solid $\text{Mg(OH)}_{2}$ out of solution.

Apply the Group 2 hydroxide trend**
Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group: $\text{Mg(OH)}_{2}$ is least soluble, $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2}$ is most soluble. $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2}$ stays dissolved in water, so mixing $\text{BaCl}_{2}(\text{aq})$ with $\text{Ca(OH)}_{2}(\text{aq})$ gives no solid.
Final answer: $\text{Ba(OH)}_{2}$ is soluble in water / solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group, so no precipitate forms.

hints: Look at the conditions and change in reaction 4: a single carbonate heated to give an oxide plus a gas, and recall the name for breakdown by heat alone.
walkthrough:
Recognise breakdown by heat**
$\text{MgCO}_{3} \rightarrow \text{MgO} + \text{CO}_{2}$. One compound is split into two simpler substances using heat only. That reaction type is called thermal decomposition.

hints: Recall what happens when $\text{Ag}^{+}$ ions meet $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ions in solution, including the colour of the silver halide formed.
Think about how that solid behaves with dilute $\text{NH}_{3}(\text{aq})$ compared with $\text{AgBr}$ and $\text{AgI}$, which need concentrated ammonia or stay insoluble.
walkthrough:
Form the silver halide**
$\text{MgCl}_{2}$ provides $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ions: $\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \text{Cl}^{-}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}(\text{s})$. Silver chloride is a white precipitate, so the colourless solution turns cloudy white.

Test with dilute ammonia**
$\text{AgCl}$ is the one silver halide that dissolves in dilute $\text{NH}_{3}(\text{aq})$ to give a colourless solution. So on adding $1 \text{ cm}^{3}$ of dilute $\text{NH}_{3}(\text{aq})$ the white solid redissolves and disappears. You must state both the white precipitate and its dissolving to gain full credit.

Final answer: White precipitate / solid forms on addition of $\text{AgNO}_{3}(\text{aq})$.
Precipitate dissolves / disappears on addition of dilute $\text{NH}_{3}(\text{aq})$.

hints: Recall the rule for halogen displacement: a halogen can only oxidise a halide ion below it in Group 17, and consider the relative positions of bromine and chlorine.
walkthrough:
Check who can oxidise whom**
Oxidising power of halogens decreases down Group 17: $\text{Cl}_{2} > \text{Br}_{2} > \text{I}_{2}$. A halogen can only displace a halide below it, for example $\text{Cl}_{2}$ oxidises $\text{Br}^{-}$ to $\text{Br}_{2}$.

Explain the orange colour staying**
Here $\text{Br}_{2}$ meets $\text{Cl}^{-}$. Because bromine is below chlorine, $\text{Br}_{2}$ is a weaker oxidising agent than $\text{Cl}_{2}$ and cannot take electrons from $\text{Cl}^{-}$. No $\text{Cl}_{2}$ forms, so no reaction happens and the orange colour of $\text{Br}_{2}(\text{aq})$ is unchanged.
Final answer: Bromine / $\text{Br}_{2}$ is too weak an oxidising agent to oxidise chloride / $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ions, so no reaction occurs and orange $\text{Br}_{2}(\text{aq})$ remains.
